title: what the double-fork?
excerpt: creating a robust posix daemon for zmx

2026-07-30 · erock's devlog

creating a robust posix daemon for zmx

•

I built zmx as a multi-faceted learning exercise. I wanted to learn more about zig, posix, daemons, ptys, libghostty, and terminals. Creating a program that fits into my core dev toolchain was merely a side-effect. While researching about how to create a daemon, buried in the implementation of abduco, I discovered the double-fork.

•

Hidden behind the double-fork technique is a cascade of terms and concepts that are fundamental to how linux manages processes. This post is me coming to the surface and intended to be a reminder when I read zmx and say "what the double-fork?"

what is a daemon?

•

A daemon belongs to a session that has no controlling terminal. For example, when you background a process using ctrl-z+bg or {cmd} &, the session still has a controlling terminal which means it can control those background processes. This is not ideal for a daemon.

•

There are other ways to background a process that does disconnect it from the terminal, with varying degress of pros and cons:

•

nohup {cmd} &

•

setsid {cmd} &

•

{cmd} & disown

how does fork work in a program?

•

When using fork(2) in a program, it will create a child process in addition to still running the parent process that called fork. This was hard for me to grok when building out zmx. It is as-if the program clones itself at that exact line and both copies continue independently from there. Typically when creating a daemon you would use the child process of the fork and then kill the parent process.

•

                       fork()
                         │
            ┌────────────┴────────────┐
            ▼                         ▼
   ┌─────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────┐
   │    PARENT       │       │    CHILD        │
   │    PID = 42     │       │    PID = 55     │
   │    PPID = 10    │       │    PPID = 42    │
   │                 │       │                 │
   │  (continues     │       │  (continues     │
   │   from the      │       │   from the      │
   │   fork point)   │       │   fork point)   │
   └─────────────────┘       └─────────────────┘

•

Identical memory at fork point (copy-on-write)

•

Identical open file descriptors (shared offsets)

•

Different return value from fork():

•

parent → child's PID (55)

•

child → 0

•

Both run independently from here

what is a session?

•

In linux, a session is a container for process groups.

•

Process groups are a container for processes that receives signals from the same terminal.

•

At-most one process group in a session can be in the foreground.

•

It receives signals and can write to the terminal.

•

All other process groups in the session are background, and SIGTTOU/SIGTTIN will stop them if they write to or read from the terminal.

•

session/
├── process group (foreground)
│   ├── process
│   ├── process
│   └── process
└── process group (background)
    ├── process
    └── process

what is a controlling terminal?

•

Only a session leader can create a controlling terminal for the session.

•

A session can have at-most one controlling terminal.

•

The session leader that opens the terminal becomes the controlling process.

why double-fork?

•

When launching a daemon, you normally set the child process of the fork to be the session leader via setsid() which creates a new session that removes the current controlling terminal. This is important because we don't want a controlling terminal for our daemon or else it could receive signals to shutdown when the controlling terminal closes.

•

However, if the first fork's child process is also the daemon process, then it's technically possible for the daemon to open a terminal device (e.g. open("/dev/console", O_RDWR)) and then it would acquire a controlling terminal! A controlling terminal would expose the daemon to terminal-generated signals (e.g. SIGINT) or SIGHUP from terminal disconnect which could kill the daemon.

•

The first fork produces a child guaranteed not to be a group leader, so setsid() will succeed. By forking a second time, the grandchild process (the daemon) is not the session leader. Per POSIX, only a process that is the session leader can acquire a controlling terminal.

•

Apparently this is "a bit paranoid" and on Linux it is arguable since a session leader only acquires a controlling terminal under implementation-defined conditions. But the double-fork is the portable way to guarantee the daemon can never acquire one, regardless of how a given POSIX implementation behaves. So we baked it into zmx.

•

PID=42  SID=10  PGID=10  ← original (PG leader, has tty)
    │
    │  fork #1
    ├──────────┐
    │ exit     │ PID=55  SID=10  PGID=10  (not a PG leader)
    ✝          │
               │ setsid()
               ▼
              PID=55  SID=55  PGID=55  (session leader, no tty)
                │
                │  fork #2
                ├──────────┐
                │ exit     │ PID=73  SID=55  PGID=55
                ✝          │ PID≠SID → can't get a tty
                           ▼
                         DAEMON ✓

beyond the double-fork

•

The double-fork detaches the daemon from any controlling terminal, but that's only one piece of a robust daemon. A daemon also needs to clean up everything it inherited from the parent that launched it like file descriptors, working directory, and standard streams.

•

In zmx, after the second fork, the daemon does two more things:

•

First, it redirects stdin, stdout, and stderr to /dev/null via dup2(2). This is critical: if the parent was launched by a test harness like bats, those file descriptors might be pipes. As long as the daemon holds the write end open, the harness will hang waiting for EOF. Redirecting to /dev/null closes that loop.

•

Second, it closes all inherited file descriptors from 3 up to 64 (skipping any that the caller explicitly wants to keep, like a server socket). This releases resources the daemon doesn't need and prevents the same hang on higher-numbered FDs.

•

We do *not* chdir because opening a shell in the cwd is a feature of zmx

•

We do *not* umask mainly because it has never been an issue

•

[1] fork()          ── child is not a PG leader
[2] setsid()        ── new session, drop tty, become leader
[3] fork()          ── daemon is not the leader, can't get tty
─────────── double-fork ends, cleanup begins ───────────
[4] chdir("/")      ── don't pin a mount point
[5] umask(0)        ── predictable file-creation modes
[6] dup2 /dev/null  ── stdin/stdout/stderr → /dev/null
[7] close fds 3-64  ── release inherited resources

preferred ways to daemon a process

•

Ideally you would be able to create a daemon using your OS supervisor like systemd, openrc, runit, etc. This was not a great option for zmx because I wanted it to be portable on linux and mac. I also wanted zmx to "just work" by auto-daemonizing the session during attach. So in the case of zmx, when we fork, the child process becomes the daemon and the parent process becomes the client that connects to the daemon via a unix socket.

blocks.html_en: First, it redirects stdin, stdout, and stderr to /dev/null via dup2(2). This is critical: if the parent was launched by a test harness like bats, those file descriptors might be pipes. As long as the daemon holds the write end open, the harness will hang waiting for EOF. Redirecting to /dev/null closes that loop.

sentences.en: First, it redirects stdin, stdout, and stderr to /dev/null via dup2(2).
sentences.zh: 首先，它通过 dup2(2) 将 stdin、stdout 和 stderr 重定向到 /dev/null。

sentences.en: This is critical: if the parent was launched by a test harness like bats, those file descriptors might be pipes.
sentences.zh: 这很关键：如果父级是由像 bats 这样的测试工具启动的，那么这些文件描述符可能是管道。

sentences.en: As long as the daemon holds the write end open, the harness will hang waiting for EOF.
sentences.zh: 只要守护进程保持写入端打开，线束就会挂起等待 EOF。

sentences.en: Redirecting to /dev/null closes that loop.
sentences.zh: 重定向到 /dev/null 将关闭该循环。

blocks.html_en: Second, it closes all inherited file descriptors from 3 up to 64 (skipping any that the caller explicitly wants to keep, like a server socket). This releases resources the daemon doesn't need and prevents the same hang on higher-numbered FDs.

sentences.en: Second, it closes all inherited file descriptors from 3 up to 64 (skipping any that the caller explicitly wants to keep, like a server socket).
sentences.zh: 其次，它关闭从 3 到 64 的所有继承文件描述符（跳过调用者明确想要保留的任何文件描述符，例如服务器套接字）。

sentences.en: This releases resources the daemon doesn't need and prevents the same hang on higher-numbered FDs.
sentences.zh: 这会释放守护程序不需要的资源，并防止在编号较大的 FD 上出现同样的挂起情况。

blocks.html_en: We do *not* chdir because opening a shell in the cwd is a feature of zmx

sentences.en: We do *not* chdir because opening a shell in the cwd is a feature of zmx
sentences.zh: 我们*不* chdir 因为在 cwd 中打开 shell 是 zmx 的一个功能

blocks.html_en: We do *not* umask mainly because it has never been an issue

sentences.en: We do *not* umask mainly because it has never been an issue
sentences.zh: 我们*不* umask 主要是因为它从来都不是一个问题

blocks.html_en: preferred ways to daemon a process

sentences.en: preferred ways to daemon a process
sentences.zh: 守护进程的首选方法

blocks.html_en: Ideally you would be able to create a daemon using your OS supervisor like systemd, openrc, runit, etc. This was not a great option for zmx because I wanted it to be portable on linux and mac. I also wanted zmx to "just work" by auto-daemonizing the session during attach. So in the case of zmx, when we fork, the child process becomes the daemon and the parent process becomes the client that connects to the daemon via a unix socket.

sentences.zh: 理想情况下，您将能够使用操作系统管理程序（例如 systemd、openrc、runit 等）创建守护程序。这对于 zmx 来说不是一个很好的选择，因为我希望它能够在 Linux 和 Mac 上移植。

sentences.zh: 我还希望 zmx 通过在附加过程中自动守护会话来“正常工作”。

content_html_zh:
2026-07-30 · erock 的开发日志

为 zmx 创建一个强大的 posix 守护进程

•

我将 zmx 构建为多方面的学习练习。 我想了解有关 zig、posix、守护进程、ptys、libghostty 和终端的更多信息。 创建一个适合我的核心开发工具链的程序只是一个副作用。 在研究如何创建守护进程（埋藏在 abduco 的实现中）时，我发现了双分叉。

•

双分叉技术背后隐藏着一系列术语和概念，它们是 Linux 管理进程的基础。 这篇文章是我浮出水面的，目的是当我读到 zmx 并说“双分叉是什么？”时提醒我。

什么是守护进程？

•

守护程序属于没有控制终端的会话。 例如，当您使用 ctrl-z+bg 或 {cmd} & 将进程后台化时，会话仍然具有控制终端，这意味着它可以控制这些后台进程。 这对于守护进程来说并不理想。

•

还有其他方法可以将进程置于后台，从而将其与终端断开连接，各有不同程度的优缺点：

•

nohup {cmd} &

•

setid {cmd} &

•

{cmd} 并否认

fork 在程序中如何工作？

•

当在程序中使用 fork(2) 时，除了仍然运行调用 fork 的父进程之外，它还会创建一个子进程。 在构建 zmx 时，这对我来说很难理解。 就好像程序在该行克隆了自己，并且两个副本都从那里独立地继续。 通常，在创建守护进程时，您会使用 fork 的子进程，然后终止父进程。

•

                       fork()
                         │
            ┌────────────┴────────────┐
            ▼                         ▼
   ┌─────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────┐
   │    PARENT       │       │    CHILD        │
   │    PID = 42     │       │    PID = 55     │
   │    PPID = 10    │       │    PPID = 42    │
   │                 │       │                 │
   │  (continues     │       │  (continues     │
   │   from the      │       │   from the      │
   │   fork point)   │       │   fork point)   │
   └─────────────────┘       └─────────────────┘

•

分叉点的相同内存（写时复制）

•

相同的打开文件描述符（共享偏移量）

•

与 fork() 不同的返回值：

•

父级 → 子级的 PID (55)

•

child → 0

•

两者都从这里独立运行

什么是会话？

•

在linux中，会话是进程组的容器。

•

进程组是从同一终端接收信号的进程的容器。

•

会话中最多可以有一个进程组位于前台。

•

它接收信号并可以写入终端。

•

会话中的所有其他进程组都是后台的，如果它们向终端写入或从终端读取，SIGTTOU/SIGTTIN 将停止它们。

•

session/
├── process group (foreground)
│   ├── process
│   ├── process
│   └── process
└── process group (background)
    ├── process
    └── process

什么是控制终端？

•

只有会话领导者才能创建会话的控制终端。

•

一个会话最多可以有一个控制终端。

•

打开终端的会话领导者成为控制进程。

为什么要双叉？

•

启动守护进程时，通常通过setsid()将fork的子进程设置为会话领导者，这会创建一个新会话，删除当前的控制终端。 这很重要，因为我们不希望守护进程有一个控制终端，否则当控制终端关闭时它可能会收到关闭信号。

•

但是，如果第一个 fork 的子进程也是守护进程，那么从技术上来说，守护进程可以打开终端设备（例如 open("/dev/console", O_RDWR)），然后它将获取控制终端！ 控制终端会将守护进程暴露给终端生成的信号（例如 SIGINT）或来自终端断开连接的 SIGHUP，这可能会杀死守护进程。

•

第一个分叉产生的子代保证不会成为组长，因此 setsid() 将会成功。 通过第二次分叉，孙进程（守护进程）不再是会话领导者。 根据 POSIX，只有作为会话领导者的进程才能获取控制终端。

•

显然，这“有点偏执”，并且在 Linux 上这是有争议的，因为会话领导者仅在实现定义的条件下获取控制终端。 但双分叉是一种可移植的方式，可以保证守护进程永远无法获取守护进程，无论给定的 POSIX 实现如何运行。 所以我们将它烘焙到zmx中。

•

PID=42  SID=10  PGID=10  ← original (PG leader, has tty)
    │
    │  fork #1
    ├──────────┐
    │ exit     │ PID=55  SID=10  PGID=10  (not a PG leader)
    ✝          │
               │ setsid()
               ▼
              PID=55  SID=55  PGID=55  (session leader, no tty)
                │
                │  fork #2
                ├──────────┐
                │ exit     │ PID=73  SID=55  PGID=55
                ✝          │ PID≠SID → can't get a tty
                           ▼
                         DAEMON ✓

超越双叉

•

双分叉将守护进程与任何控制终端分离，但这只是强大守护进程的一部分。 守护进程还需要清理从启动它的父进程继承的所有内容，例如文件描述符、工作目录和标准流。

•

在 zmx 中，在第二次 fork 之后，守护进程还做了两件事：

•

首先，它通过 dup2(2) 将 stdin、stdout 和 stderr 重定向到 /dev/null。 这很关键：如果父级是由像 bats 这样的测试工具启动的，那么这些文件描述符可能是管道。 只要守护进程保持写入端打开，线束就会挂起等待 EOF。 重定向到 /dev/null 将关闭该循环。

•

其次，它关闭从 3 到 64 的所有继承文件描述符（跳过调用者明确想要保留的任何文件描述符，例如服务器套接字）。 这会释放守护程序不需要的资源，并防止在编号较大的 FD 上出现同样的挂起情况。

•

我们*不* chdir 因为在 cwd 中打开 shell 是 zmx 的一个功能

•

我们*不* umask 主要是因为它从来都不是一个问题

•

[1] fork()          ── child is not a PG leader
[2] setsid()        ── new session, drop tty, become leader
[3] fork()          ── daemon is not the leader, can't get tty
─────────── double-fork ends, cleanup begins ───────────
[4] chdir("/")      ── don't pin a mount point
[5] umask(0)        ── predictable file-creation modes
[6] dup2 /dev/null  ── stdin/stdout/stderr → /dev/null
[7] close fds 3-64  ── release inherited resources

守护进程的首选方法

•

理想情况下，您将能够使用操作系统管理程序（例如 systemd、openrc、runit 等）创建守护程序。这对于 zmx 来说不是一个很好的选择，因为我希望它能够在 Linux 和 Mac 上移植。 我还希望 zmx 通过在附加过程中自动守护会话来“正常工作”。 因此，在 zmx 的情况下，当我们 fork 时，子进程成为守护进程，父进程成为通过 unix 套接字连接到守护进程的客户端。
